content: The Dapivirine vaginal ring has been extensively studied as a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) method to prevent HIV infection among women at high risk. Below are detailed findings from various studies and trials: 1. Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Fonner and Dalglish conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy of the Dapivirine vaginal ring in preventing HIV among women at substantial risk of infection. This work remains unpublished but highlights the potential of the ring as a preventive tool. 2. Social Harms and Adherence: Palanee-Phillips et al. investigated the impact of partner-related social harms on women’s adherence to the Dapivirine vaginal ring during a Phase III trial. Their findings, published in J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr (2018), emphasize the importance of addressing social dynamics to improve adherence. 3. Hormonal Contraception Compatibility: Balkus et al. demonstrated that the use of the Dapivirine vaginal ring does not compromise the effectiveness of hormonal contraception. This study, published in J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr (2017), supports the ring’s compatibility with other reproductive health interventions. 4. Pregnancy and Infant Outcomes: Makanani et al. assessed pregnancy and infant outcomes among women who used the Dapivirine vaginal ring during early pregnancy. Their findings, published in J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr (2018), provide critical safety data for this population. 5. HIV Prevention in Uganda: Kusemererwa and Abasa edited a study on the incidence and outcomes of pregnancy among women using the Dapivirine vaginal ring in a Phase III trial in southwestern Uganda. Published in AIDS Res Hum Retrovir (2018), this work highlights the ring’s role in HIV prevention in resource-limited settings. 6. Behavioral Impact: Another study edited by Kusemererwa and Abasa explored whether the use of the Dapivirine vaginal ring leads to changes in risky sexual behavior. Published in AIDS Res Hum Retrovir (2018), the findings suggest no significant behavioral disinhibition associated with ring use. 7. Modeling Health Outcomes: Glaubius et al. modeled the health outcomes, drug resistance, and cost-effectiveness of the Dapivirine vaginal ring for HIV prevention. Published in J Int AIDS Soc (2019), this study underscores the ring’s potential as a cost-effective intervention. 8. Cost-Effectiveness Analysis: Smith et al. conducted a modeling analysis to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of the intravaginal Dapivirine ring. Their findings, accessible via Cochrane Central, highlight the economic viability of this intervention. 9. Postmenopausal Women: Chen et al. conducted a Phase 2a safety, pharmacokinetics, and acceptability study of the Dapivirine vaginal ring in postmenopausal women in the U.S. Published in Clin Infect Dis (2019), this study expands the ring’s potential use to older populations. 10. Adolescents and Young Women: Bunge et al. conducted a Phase IIa safety study of the Dapivirine vaginal ring in adolescent young women. Published in J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr (2020), this study provides critical data on the ring’s safety in younger populations. 11. Acceptability in Lowand Middle-Income Countries: Griffin et al. performed a systematic review and narrative synthesis on the acceptability and preferences for vaginal rings among women in lowand middle-income countries. Published in PLoS One (2019), this study highlights cultural and contextual factors influencing ring use. 12. End-User Perspectives: Schwartz et al. explored end-user perspectives on their ability, motivation, and opportunity to use the Dapivirine vaginal ring. Presented at the 23rd International AIDS Conference (2020), this study provides insights into user experiences and barriers. 13. Initial Impressions and Adherence: Van der Straten et al. examined how initial worries about the Dapivirine vaginal ring influence adherence. Published in J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr (2019), this study emphasizes the importance of addressing user concerns early. 14. Negative Rumors: Chitukuta et al. investigated the impact of negative rumors about the vaginal ring for HIV-1 prevention in sub-Saharan Africa. Published in Culture Health Sexuality (2019), this study highlights the role of misinformation in shaping perceptions and adherence. 15. Menstrual-Related Removal: Duby et al. explored why women removed the Dapivirine vaginal ring during menstruation in Malawi, South Africa, Uganda, and Zimbabwe. Published in AIDS Behav (2020), this study identifies hygiene and comfort concerns as key factors. 16. Impact on Sexual Experiences: Laborde et al. examined the impact of the Dapivirine vaginal ring on sexual experiences and intimate partnerships. Published in AIDS Behav (2018), this study discusses how ring detection and sexual dynamics influence user experiences. 17. Disclosure to Male Partners: Nair et al. studied the disclosure of vaginal ring use to male partners in an HIV prevention study and its impact on adherence. Published in AIDS Res Hum Retrovir (2018), this study highlights the importance of partner communication. 18. Safety and Pharmacokinetics: Nel et al. conducted a safety and pharmacokinetic trial assessing the delivery of Dapivirine from a vaginal ring in healthy women. Published in AIDS (2014), this foundational study provides critical data on the ring’s safety profile. 19. Global Contraceptive Use: Ross and Stover analyzed evidence from 1982–2009, demonstrating that the availability of more contraceptive methods increases modern contraceptive use. Published in Global Health: Science and Practice (2013), this study supports the integration of the Dapivirine ring into broader reproductive health strategies. 20. Point-of-Care Infant Diagnosis: WHO guidelines recommend point-of-care nucleic acid testing for diagnosing HIV in infants under 18 months. This approach significantly reduces the time to diagnosis and treatment initiation, as evidenced by systematic reviews and studies across sub-Saharan Africa. 21. Cost-Effectiveness of Point-of-Care Testing: Studies consistently show that point-of-care testing is more cost-effective than laboratory-based testing, with significant health benefits such as life-years saved and deaths averted. Integration across diseases further enhances cost savings. 22. Implementation Challenges: Despite its benefits, challenges remain in scaling up point-of-care testing, including costs, infrastructure, and access. Efforts must focus on reducing costs and increasing availability in high-burden settings. These findings collectively underscore the Dapivirine vaginal ring’s potential as a safe, effective, and acceptable HIV prevention method, while also highlighting the need for continued research, education, and infrastructure development to maximize its impact.
